note: Korean has no verb 'to have' for possession in everyday speech. 'I have time' is 시간이 있어요 — 'time exists (for me).' The owner is just understood.
맛 (taste) + 있다 (exists). Its opposite, 맛없어요, is literally 'taste doesn't exist' = it tastes bad. The 'exists' pattern builds many words.
Koreans say 'our' for things tied to a shared group — family, home, country, company — even when speaking only for themselves. Saying 내 엄마 ('my mom') sounds oddly possessive.
The body part is the subject: 배 (stomach/belly) + 고프다. No 'I' needed — context supplies it. Same family: 배불러요 ('stomach is full') = I'm full.
Qualities are often expressed through body parts: a good head = intelligence. Its cousin 눈이 높다 ('eyes are high') means having picky standards.
A warm everyday greeting, historically rooted in times when a full meal wasn't guaranteed. Nobody is actually asking about your meal — answer 네 (yes) and greet back.
Said before a meal to the cook or host — gratitude packaged as a promise. Its bookend, 잘 먹었습니다 ('I ate well'), is said after finishing.

real: good work today / thanks for your effort
note: The standard sign-off with coworkers, staff, or anyone who did work — acknowledging effort itself rather than results. English has no everyday equivalent.

real: you can do it! / good luck!
note: Borrowed from English 'fighting' but repurposed as pure encouragement — before exams, interviews, games. Nothing combative about it.

real: this hits the spot (even about hot soup!)
note: Famously said while eating scalding-hot soup or sitting in a hot bath. It describes the refreshed, unblocked feeling — not the temperature.
Between neighbors and acquaintances this is often just a greeting, not an interrogation. A vague answer like 그냥요 ('just...') is completely fine.

real: the art of reading a room
note: The skill of sensing others' moods and the unspoken situation. You can have fast 눈치, lack it (눈치 없다), or 'see 눈치' (눈치를 보다) — anxiously gauging others' reactions.

real: deep attachment that grows over time
note: The bond that accumulates between people who share time — friends, family, even a grumpy neighbor. You can have 정 for someone you don't especially like. It explains a lot of Korean social life.
The specific feeling of a blocked chest: slow wifi, a friend who won't take advice, a stuck situation, an airless room. Physical and emotional at once — English needs a whole sentence for it.
The soft regret when something good ends too soon or almost worked out — leaving a great trip, losing narrowly, a friend moving away. Not sad exactly; wistful.
The universal answer to 'why?' when there is no why. 왜 왔어요? (Why'd you come?) — 그냥. It deflects gently without being rude. Massively common in real speech.
도 doesn't stack on the particles you know — it replaces them. 음악을도 is wrong; the single 도 carries both the 'object' job and the 'also' job at once.

real: headed there vs. doing something there
note: 에 points at a destination (or where something exists); 에서 marks where an action happens. 학교에 가요 — go TO school. 학교에서 공부해요 — study AT school. Mixing them is the classic learner tell.
One particle, two English jobs. Between nouns it's 'and': 우유하고 빵 (milk and bread). After a noun, before the action, it's 'with': 친구하고 봤어요 (watched it with a friend). Context decides.
The standard greeting after time apart — the past tense of 지내다 (to spend time / get along). Answer by bouncing it back: 네, 잘 지냈어요.

English 'don't' blurs what Korean splits: 안 is a decision, 못 is inability or circumstance. 술 안 마셔요 — I choose not to drink. 술 못 마셔요 — I can't (health, driving, tolerance). Koreans hear the difference instantly.

real: I want vs. he/she seems to want
note: Korean grammar marks WHOSE desire it is. -고 싶어요 is for your own (or your listener's) wants; describing a third person's takes -고 싶어해요 — you can only report the wanting they display, not feel it for them.

치킨 + 맥주 squashed into one word — a whole social institution: after-work gatherings, summer river picnics, watching the game. Korean loves these portmanteaus; learn the parts and you can often decode the whole.

real: which word depends on YOUR gender
note: Korean has four words where English has two: a woman's older sister is 언니, a man's is 누나; a woman's older brother is 오빠, a man's is 형. And they stretch past blood — close older friends earn the same titles. Age ordering is social infrastructure.
The ritual invitation to switch from polite speech into 반말 — you 'put down' the formal language like a heavy bag. Until someone says this (or you're clearly the elder), stay in -요.

real: the same word, worn formal or plain
note: Honorifics swap whole NOUNS, not just verb endings: an elder's age is 연세, their meal is 진지, their house is 댁. You'll ask a friend's 나이 but a grandmother's 연세 — same question, different wardrobe.

real: 10:10 — two number systems on one clock face
note: Korean runs both number systems at once and the clock splits them down the middle: hours are native (열 시), minutes are Sino (십 분). Nobody knows a tidy reason; everybody does it anyway. Say a full time and you've used both systems in four syllables.

약속 있어요 sounds like you've sworn an oath; it means you have dinner plans. The word covers everything from pinky promises to calendar entries — commitments big and small share one word, which says something about how seriously plans are taken.

real: the old count-from-one system (now mostly retired)
note: Traditionally you were born at one 살 and everyone aged together on New Year's — so 'Korean age' ran one or two years ahead of international age. A 2023 law standardized the international count (만 나이), but the old system lingers in conversation, so you'll still hear both.

real: near me / near YOU / far from us both
note: English splits space two ways; Korean splits it three: 여기 is by the speaker, 거기 is by the listener, 저기 is away from both. That's why 거기 is also 'there (where you are)' on the phone — and why pointing across the room is always 저기.

lit: go to school / go toward school
note: 에 pins the destination — you end up at school. (으)로 gives the bearing — you head that way, no promise you stop there. Taxi Korean runs on (으)로: 왼쪽으로, 오른쪽으로, 역으로 (station-ward).

English parts, Korean invention — no English speaker says 'hand phone.' Konglish is its own vocabulary layer: 아파트 (apartment building), 서비스 (a freebie on the house), 파이팅 (you can do it!). Knowing English helps — and misleads.

real: I'm fine / it's okay / no thanks
note: One word, three jobs: comfort someone (it's okay!), answer 'how are you' (I'm fine), and — the one that trips learners — politely DECLINE. Offered a bag at the checkout, 괜찮아요 means 'no thanks.' Watch the hand-wave that comes with it.

The older word 푸르다 covered sky, sea, AND forests, and that range still echoes: a green traffic light is 파란불 ('blue light') and lush mountains are 푸른 산. 초록색 is unambiguously green — but don't be surprised when Korean calls the go-light blue.

Korean mass-produces adjectives by declaring existence: taste exists (delicious), fun exists (interesting), problem doesn't exist (no problem), 멋있다 — style exists (cool). Learn 있다/없다 once and whole families of words assemble themselves.

real: I'll be busy — or she's probably busy
note: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 does two jobs: about yourself it's a plan (갈 거예요 — I'm going to go); about others or the world it's an educated guess (지금 바쁠 거예요 — she's probably busy). Same ending, plan or prediction — who the subject is decides.

이 is the number two, a tooth, 'this' (coming soon), the subject particle, and a common surname (Lee). Hanja once told them apart in writing; in speech, context has always done the work. Korean's short syllables moonlight shamelessly — meet each 이 as its own word.

Doubling for urgency — 빨리 (fast) said twice is a whole national tempo: same-day delivery, sprint-speed service, elevators with worn-out door-close buttons. Koreans joke about it and take quiet pride in it. You'll hear it before you learn it formally.

real: a statement about an elder — or a request to you
note: The same -(으)세요 ending honors the subject (선생님이 가세요 — the teacher is going) AND makes polite requests (가세요 — please go). Context and intonation decide. It's why 안녕히 가세요 — goodbye — is literally 'please go peacefully.'

좀 is 조금 (a little) worn smooth — but in requests it isn't about quantity. It's a cushion, like English 'just' or 'could you…': 물 좀 주세요 asks nicely, not sparingly. Sprinkle it into any 주세요 and sound instantly more native.

서비스예요! from a shop owner means a free extra just landed on your table — bonus 반찬, an extra skewer, dessert you didn't order. English 'service' got imported and promoted into generosity. Respond with delighted 감사합니다.

Korean builds 'can' out of existence: 수 is a way/means, so ability = 'the way exists' and inability = 'the way doesn't exist' (갈 수 없어요). The same 있다/없다 factory that built 맛있다 and 재미있다 — existence is Korean's favorite raw material.

되다 means become-work-be-okay, so its negation is the universal veto: rules (여기서 사진 안 돼요 — no photos here), refusals, and pure disbelief. Screamed without the 요 — 안 돼!!! — it's the sound of every K-drama's worst moment.

Compliment a Korean speaker's English and you'll hear 잘 못 해요 — regardless of fluency. Deflecting praise is good manners, not low self-esteem. When YOUR Korean gets complimented (it will — 한국어 잘하시네요!), the culturally perfect return is 아니에요, 잘 못 해요.

English needs a dummy 'it' to rain; Korean lets the weather act for itself: 비가 와요, 눈이 와요 — rain and snow are travelers that arrive. Wind gets its own verb (바람이 불어요), and rain even stops itself (비가 그쳐요). The sky is full of subjects.

real: one syllable for sky and face
note: 눈이 와요 — snow is coming. 눈이 예뻐요 — your eyes are pretty (probably). Older Korean held them apart by vowel length (snow was the long one); modern speech leans entirely on context. 눈사람 (snow-person) and 눈물 (eye-water: tears) each inherit a different 눈.

real: the summer monsoon — a season inside a season
note: For a few weeks around July, rain becomes the default state and umbrellas become clothing. 장마 has start dates, forecasts, and its own mood. Alongside 미세먼지 season and 벚꽃 season, it's proof Korea runs on many more than four seasons.
No word for 'traffic jam' needed — the road itself gets stopped up, like a pipe. The same verb clogs noses (코가 막혀요) and speechless moments (말이 막혀요). One metaphor, many blockages.

Korean rarely uses names with strangers — jobs + 님 do the work: 기사님 (driver), 사장님 (owner), 선생님 (teacher, or any respectable stranger). Address people by their role worn with honor, and doors open. Literally, sometimes.

Seoul's subway sleeps around midnight, so 막차 시간 quietly governs every evening's social physics — the glance at the phone, the 먼저 가요, the sprint through the station. Miss it and the night gets a taxi-fare surcharge.

Move into a new place and you owe your people a 집들이. Guests traditionally bring 휴지 (toilet paper) or 세제 (detergent) — long rolls and rising bubbles mean a long life and growing fortune. The host cooks; the guests admire the view; everyone asks about the rent.

Traditionally, kitchen smoke was routed under stone floors; today hot-water pipes do the job in every apartment. It's why floors are for sitting and sleeping, why an 이불 on the 바닥 beats a cold bed, and why shoes stop at the 현관 — you don't wear the street across a surface you sleep on.

real: I'm exhausted / so done with today
note: Said at desks, in classrooms, in queues — and, famously, while already at home. When there's no energy left for anything, the stated destination is 집, even if you're sitting in it. M3's -고 싶어요 doing emotional heavy-lifting.

Not quite flu, not quite fatigue: the full-body collapse Korean recognizes as its own named disease — 몸살이 났어요, and everyone nods. Doctors prescribe 푹 쉬세요; grandmothers prescribe soup. That the language needs this word says something about the work culture.

Korean hyperbole's favorite engine: [feeling] + 죽겠어요 = dying of it. 더워 죽겠어요 (dying of heat), 힘들어 죽겠어요 (dying of hardship). Nobody is dying; everybody says it hourly. English does 'starving to death' — Korean industrialized the pattern.

Said of the host who cooks for twelve when four are coming. The body is Korean's favorite metaphor kit: 코가 높다 (high nose — arrogant), 입이 무겁다 (heavy mouth — keeps secrets), 귀가 얇다 (thin ears — easily swayed). Glove size is not the point.

Korean doesn't take tests — it SEES them. 시험을 봐요 (I'm taking a test), 시험을 잘 봤어요 (it went well). English 'sits' exams in Britain and 'takes' them in America; Korean watches them happen. Same verb as seeing a movie.

real: the exam that stops the nation
note: One November morning, all of Korea holds its breath: flights are grounded during the listening section, offices open late to clear the roads, police escort late students with sirens on, and juniors cheer at the school gates. Twelve years of 학원 evenings aim at this single day.

real: you can do it! / good luck!
note: Konglish that outgrew its source: borrowed 'fighting,' repurposed as pure encouragement. Said before exams, interviews, matches, Mondays. English speakers find it adorably aggressive; Koreans find English's lack of an equivalent genuinely inconvenient.

The skill of sensing what everyone needs without being told: when to refill a glass, when the 부장님's 'anyone busy tonight?' isn't a question, when to leave. 눈치가 빠르다 — quick radar — is high praise; 눈치가 없다 is a diagnosis. Perhaps Korean's most famous untranslatable.

Said at every departure from shared work — leaving the office, ending a call, finishing a class. It doesn't evaluate the work; it honors the effort. English 'good job' judges; 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges. Learn it before your first Korean workplace; hear it forever after.

Take M5's weekday names, delete the weekend, photocopy Friday over it: the seven-day workweek as dark comedy. Office workers say it the way soldiers sing marching songs. Its existence — like 몸살's — is a cultural x-ray.
